strengths: The core metric, Visual Information Gain (VIG), is simple, well-motivated, and grounded in a clean theoretical derivation connecting it to cross-entropy loss and KL divergence, giving a principled interpretation as the reduction in prediction divergence from providing the image.

The empirical validation of VIG as an indicator of visual grounding is thorough: sample-level VIG aligns with known benchmark-level modality dependencies (COCO/POPE vs. GQA/SQA), and token-level VIG cleanly separates visually grounded content words (colors, poses) from function words (articles, prepositions), which is intuitive and convincing.

The selective training scheme is tested across three different model/scale combinations (LLaVA-1.5 7B, 13B, ShareGPT4V 7B) and consistently improves performance while using substantially fewer tokens (e.g., 12.14M vs 58.61M for the 13B model), demonstrating good data efficiency.

Comparisons against multiple existing bias-mitigation baselines (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING) show that VIG training is competitive or superior without architectural changes or inference overhead, and is shown to be complementary/orthogonal to these methods when combined.

Mechanistic analyses (attention allocation to visual tokens across layers, and robustness to textual corruption/'blind faith in text') provide converging evidence that the method changes model behavior in the intended direction, not just aggregate benchmark numbers.
Ablations on selection level (sample-only vs. sample+token) and selection ratio p are included, supporting the necessity of both components and giving some sense of sensitivity to the hyperparameter.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: thresholds, hyperparameters, training time, and qualitative examples are reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: The 'no-image' condition used to compute VIG relies on Gaussian-blurred images (following prior work), which may retain low-frequency visual cues (color palette, coarse scene layout); this could bias VIG scores in ways not analyzed, and no alternative ablation-free image removal (e.g., black/masked image, text-only forward pass) is compared to test sensitivity of the metric to this design choice.

Several evaluation benchmarks used are quite small (LLaVA-Bench-in-the-Wild has 60 questions, MM-Vet 218 questions) and are scored by LLM judges (GPT-4/GPT-3.5) known to have run-to-run variance; the paper reports single-run point estimates with no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess whether the often small reported gains (e.g., +0.03 POPE F1, +0.20 DocVQA accuracy) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The threshold τ_p is reused for both sample- and token-level selection to avoid extra hyperparameters, but the derived τ_70 values differ substantially and even in sign across models (-0.021, 0.046, -0.042), and there is no ablation decoupling sample- and token-level thresholds to show that this coupling is actually optimal rather than just convenient.

The paper does not compare VIG-based selection against simpler perplexity/loss-based data selection baselines that do not require a separate 'without-image' forward pass (e.g., selecting samples/tokens by absolute loss, by length, or by difficulty), so it is unclear how much of the benefit comes specifically from the visual contrast versus generic difficulty-based curriculum/data pruning effects.

All experiments are conducted on the LLaVA-1.5/ShareGPT4V architecture family sharing similar backbones (Vicuna + CLIP), despite the related work section referencing more modern architectures (Qwen2-VL, InternVL); generalization to different vision encoders, connector designs, or larger/more recent LVLMs is not empirically tested, limiting the evidence for broad applicability.

The claim that VIG training 'improves visual grounding' rests substantially on proxy signals (attention-to-image ratio, corrupted-text robustness) rather than more direct grounding tests (e.g., localization, referring expression accuracy), leaving some ambiguity about whether the underlying mechanism is genuinely enhanced visual reliance or simply reduced overfitting to generic textual patterns in the (now smaller, filtered) answer distribution.

The computational overhead discussion is somewhat understated; while framed as a 'one-time cost,' VIG computation requires additional forward passes with both blurred and real images over the entire training set using the aligned model, and no wall-clock/FLOP comparison against baseline data-selection costs is given to substantiate practicality at larger scale.

strengths: The core idea—explicitly quantifying per-sample and per-token visual dependency via a perplexity log-ratio—is intuitive and provides a model-agnostic lens for analyzing language bias, which is a worthwhile data-centric complement to prior architectural/decoding-based approaches.

The paper derives VIG's connection to cross-entropy and KL divergence, giving some theoretical grounding, and the token-level decomposition (Eq. 6-7) nicely unifies sample- and token-level selection under one framework without extra hyperparameters.

Evaluation spans three backbones (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B), seven benchmarks, and includes informative ablations (random vs. sample-only vs. sample+token selection; sweep over selection ratio p) as well as comparisons against four competing bias-mitigation methods (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING), showing the method is largely additive/orthogonal to them.

Analyses beyond accuracy (attention-fraction-to-image-tokens, robustness to textual corruption/'blind faith in text') offer plausible mechanistic support for the claim that VIG training increases visual grounding, not just benchmark score.
weaknesses: The entire framework hinges on simulating 'no image' via Gaussian-blurred input (borrowed from prior work) rather than a true text-only forward pass; blurring does not remove all visual cues (global color/layout statistics survive), so PPL(A|Q) is an approximate and potentially biased proxy, yet no sensitivity analysis or alternative visual-ablation strategy (e.g., masked/black image, true text-only LM) is reported to validate robustness of VIG to this choice.

Reusing the identical sample-level threshold τp for token-level masking is presented as a 'parameter-free' design, but Table 3 shows this produces wildly different effective token-retention rates across models for the same nominal p=70% sample selection (66% active tokens for 7B vs. only 21% for 13B vs. 65% for ShareGPT4V), meaning the amount of token-level pruning is effectively uncontrolled and inconsistent across settings—undermining fair cross-model comparison and the claim that a single ratio p generalizes cleanly.

Several headline gains in Table 3 are very small (e.g., +0.03 POPE F1, +0.20 DocVQA accuracy) and are reported from what appears to be single training runs with no variance/seed information, significance testing, or confidence intervals, making it hard to distinguish genuine improvement from noise, especially given that LLaVA-W (one of the primary vision-understanding benchmarks) contains only 24 images/60 questions.

The VIG scores used for selection are computed from the pre-instruction-tuned (alignment-only) model, which has not yet learned the task distribution of instruction-following; it is unclear whether 'visual dependency' as judged by this undertrained model reliably predicts which samples/tokens are valuable for downstream instruction-tuned behavior, and no ablation tests using the fully-tuned model's VIG (or iterative re-scoring) is provided.

Table 4's combination results (e.g., 'VIG training + LACING') are presented as the strongest configuration, but since this just stacks two independent interventions without deeper analysis of interaction effects, the comparison risks over-claiming synergy; moreover the baselines mix training-free and training-based methods with different costs, and no inference-time/training-time cost comparison is tabulated in the main paper.

Key design components (blurred-image surrogate, selective token masking during LM training) are directly adapted from prior work (Xing et al. for blur, Lin et al. for 'not all tokens' selective LM training), so the paper's novelty lies mainly in combining these existing ideas for the multimodal setting rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

The qualitative validation of VIG as a grounding measure (Table 1, Table 2) relies on a handful of cherry-picked examples rather than any quantitative correlation with human-judged visual grounding or hallucination labels, leaving the central claim that 'VIG reliably reflects visual dependency' insufficiently substantiated beyond benchmark-level distributional trends in Fig. 2.

strengths: The core contribution, Visual Information Gain (VIG), is a simple, interpretable, and theoretically grounded metric (perplexity ratio decomposed into KL-divergence terms) that requires no architectural modification.

The paper provides convincing multi-level validation of the metric: sample-level alignment with known benchmark modality dependencies (COCO/POPE vs GQA/SQA), token-level qualitative examples (colors, spatial relations vs. function words), and a controlled experiment varying only the image while fixing text (Table 1).

The selective training scheme is practically useful, demonstrating strong data efficiency: training on far fewer tokens (e.g., 12.14M vs 58.61M for LLaVA-1.5 13B) while improving performance across both vision-understanding and hallucination benchmarks.

Broad empirical coverage: results are reported across three different model/scale combinations (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B), 7 benchmarks, and multiple ablations (selection level, selection ratio), which strengthens generality of claims within the LLaVA/ShareGPT4V family.

Comparison against four competitive baselines (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING) shows the method is not only competitive but also complementary/orthogonal to existing training-free and training-based debiasing techniques.

Additional mechanistic analyses (attention-to-image ratio, resistance to textual corruption/"blind faith in text") provide converging evidence that the proposed training indeed increases visual grounding rather than just improving benchmark numbers through overfitting.
Good reproducibility support: appendix details thresholds, training hyperparameters, compute budget, and dataset construction.
weaknesses: The proxy for "no visual information" (Gaussian-blurred image) may still leak coarse visual cues (color, layout), which could bias VIG scores in ways not fully explored or ablated against alternative no-image proxies (e.g., black/noise image, text-only).

VIG is computed using the model after only the pre-training (alignment) stage, before instruction tuning; this could be a biased/weak proxy for how a fully instruction-tuned model actually depends on vision, and the paper does not test sensitivity of results to this choice.

The decision to reuse the same threshold τp for both sample- and token-level selection is justified primarily by avoiding extra hyperparameters rather than by evidence that this choice is optimal; no ablation varies these independently.

Many reported improvements are small in absolute terms (e.g., +0.03 F1, +0.20 Acc on DocVQA) and no variance/multiple-seed information is given, making it hard to assess statistical significance of some gains.

Some evaluation benchmarks used (e.g., LLaVA-Bench-in-the-Wild with only 24 images/60 questions, GPT-4-judged) are small and potentially noisy, and all qualitative/judged metrics rely solely on GPT-4 without human verification.

Generalization is only demonstrated within the LLaVA-1.5/ShareGPT4V model family (same CLIP+Vicuna backbone); it remains unclear whether VIG and the selection scheme transfer to architecturally different LVLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL, InternVL) as acknowledged only briefly in the limitations.

The computational overhead of computing VIG (extra forward passes per sample) is noted but not quantified relative to total training cost savings, making it hard to judge the net efficiency benefit end-to-end.

strengths: Introduces a simple, well-motivated, and theoretically grounded metric (VIG) that decomposes cleanly into a KL-divergence interpretation and token-level loss differences, giving both sample- and token-level granularity.

Extensive empirical validation of VIG as a diagnostic tool: qualitative examples with controlled image swaps (Tab. 1), benchmark-level distribution analysis aligning with known modality dependency (Fig. 2), and POS-tag/token-level analysis (Fig. 3, 4, Tab. 2) that convincingly show VIG highlights visually salient words (colors, nouns, attributes) versus function words.

Strong and broad empirical results: VIG-guided selective training improves performance while using substantially fewer active tokens (34-79% reduction) across four different model/architecture combinations (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V, Open-Qwen2VL), suggesting reasonably good generalization.
Thorough comparison against multiple existing debiasing baselines (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING), showing VIG training is competitive and orthogonal/complementary to these methods (combined gains).

Good set of ablations: selection-level ablation (sample-only vs sample+token), selection-ratio sweep, text-only benchmark preservation check, and data-distribution/long-tail analysis, which collectively support the core claims and address several natural robustness questions.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility appendix (hyperparameters, thresholds per model, compute environment, dataset details).
weaknesses: The core VIG computation depends on an ad hoc heuristic (Gaussian-blurred images) to simulate 'absence of vision,' borrowed from another paper; there is no analysis of sensitivity to blur strength or alternative no-image conditions (e.g., black image, no image token at all), which could materially affect the ranking/thresholds and downstream selection.

The method reuses a single threshold τp for both sample- and token-level selection purely to avoid extra hyperparameters, but no ablation isolates whether this joint design is actually optimal versus tuning sample and token thresholds separately; this design choice is asserted rather than justified empirically.

VIG is computed using models 'after the pre-training stage' only, and it is unclear how robust the metric/selection is to using a different or partially-trained backbone for scoring (e.g., using a stronger LLM backbone might change perplexity gaps substantially, especially since PPL-based measures can be sensitive to model calibration).

Statistical significance is not reported anywhere (single-run numbers throughout Tables 3, 4, 6, F.1, F.3); given some gains are modest (e.g., MMBench +0.87, POPE F1 +0.03), it's hard to assess whether improvements are consistently above noise, especially given LVLM instruction-tuning is known to have run-to-run variance.

The paper claims VIG-guided training 'mitigates language bias fundamentally at the representational level' but the causal mechanism is only supported by correlational analyses (attention fraction, corruption robustness); no ablation directly isolates whether gains stem from reduced language bias per se versus simply from improved data quality/curation (similar to standard data-pruning benefits unrelated to modality bias).

Baseline comparisons in Sec 4.3 are conducted only on LLaVA-1.5 7B; it remains unclear whether the competitive/complementary advantage over VCD/PAI/VAR/LACING generalizes to larger models or other architectures tested elsewhere in the paper.

The computational overhead of VIG scoring (additional forward passes per training sample) is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantified relative to the savings in training compute from token/sample pruning, making it hard to judge net efficiency gains in practice.

Some hyperparameter differences across baselines in Table 4 (e.g., LACING's own training-based tuning) may not be perfectly comparable to VIG training's setup, and the paper does not discuss whether baselines were retrained/optimized under identical compute budgets.

strengths: The proposed Visual Information Gain (VIG) metric is intuitively motivated and backed by a clean theoretical derivation connecting it to cross-entropy reduction and KL-divergence terms, giving it some principled grounding beyond an ad-hoc heuristic.

The empirical analysis in Section 3.3 (benchmark-level VIG distributions, token-level POS analysis, qualitative examples) provides reasonably convincing evidence that VIG correlates with intuitive notions of visual grounding (colors, spatial relations, object attributes vs. function words).

The method is evaluated across four different model/backbone combinations (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, Open-Qwen2VL 2B), and consistently shows improvement with substantially reduced active token counts, which is a reasonably broad empirical validation for a data-centric technique.

The paper includes useful complementary analyses: attention-fraction-to-visual-tokens, a 'blind faith in text' robustness evaluation, text-only benchmark preservation, and a long-tail/task-distribution analysis of the retained data, which together build a more complete picture of what the selection is doing.

Comparison with existing training-free and training-based debiasing baselines (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING) shows that VIG training is complementary/additive to these approaches, which is a useful practical finding.
weaknesses: The core mechanism for simulating 'absence of vision' relies on Gaussian-blurred images rather than true removal of visual conditioning; this is a crude proxy that may still leak low-level cues (color histograms, layout) and the sensitivity of VIG scores and downstream selection to the blur strength is never ablated, undermining confidence in the metric's precision.

Reusing the identical threshold τp for both sample-level and token-level selection is justified purely as a way to 'avoid introducing additional hyperparameters' rather than through any ablation showing this choice is actually optimal; given that VIG distributions differ substantially in scale between sample-level (aggregated) and token-level (per-token, much noisier) quantities, this conflation is questionable and under-justified.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or variance estimates are reported anywhere in the paper despite many reported gains being small (e.g., +0.03 F1 on POPE, +0.07 on CHAIR CI for LLaVA-1.5 13B), making it difficult to assess whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful or within noise, especially since GPT-4-based metrics (LLaVAW, MMVet, MMHal) are known to have non-trivial evaluation variance.

VIG is computed using the stage-1 'aligned' (pre-instruction-tuned) checkpoint, under the assumption that this model's visual-text correspondence meaningfully predicts which samples/tokens will be informative for the much more capable final instruction-tuned model; this assumption is not directly tested (e.g., no comparison with VIG computed from a partially instruction-tuned or fully-tuned model), leaving a potential mismatch/circularity concern.

The selection-ratio ablation (Fig. 7, Table F.3) shows inconsistent, sometimes benchmark-contradictory trends (e.g., p=30 best for LLaVAW but worse for MMBench), suggesting that the 'optimal' p is dataset/benchmark dependent; the paper does not provide a principled way to choose p without a validation sweep, which undercuts the claimed hyperparameter-simplicity of the method.

The method is essentially an application of known ideas—contrastive/PPL-based information gain (similar in spirit to contrastive decoding methods like VCD) combined with token-level selective loss masking (directly inspired by 'Not All Tokens Are What You Need' for LLMs)—to the multimodal setting; while useful, the conceptual novelty is incremental rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Comparisons are limited to the LLaVA-1.5/ShareGPT4V family plus a single smaller, less mainstream model (Open-Qwen2VL 2B); no evaluation on more recent, stronger open architectures (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL, LLaVA-OneVision) is provided, so claims of broad architecture-agnostic generalization are not fully substantiated.

No comparison against other established data-selection/pruning baselines beyond a simple random baseline (e.g., CLIP-score-based filtering, loss-based curriculum methods, or other perplexity-based selection heuristics from the LLM literature), making it hard to assess whether VIG specifically is necessary versus simpler alternatives achieving similar gains.

The computational overhead of VIG (requiring full forward passes with and without image over the entire multimodal dataset) is acknowledged but not thoroughly quantified relative to the savings obtained from training on fewer tokens, so the net efficiency claim is only partially substantiated.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually clean and theoretically grounded metric (VIG) derived from the difference in cross-entropy/perplexity with and without visual conditioning, with a clear decomposition into KL-divergence terms that gives the metric interpretability at both sample and token granularity.

Extensive empirical validation of the metric itself: benchmark-level VIG distributions align with known modality dependency differences (COCO/CV-Bench/POPE vs GQA/SQA), and token-level/POS analyses convincingly show that high-VIG tokens correspond to visually grounded content words (colors, objects, spatial terms) while low-VIG tokens are function words.

Strong and consistent practical results across four different LVLM backbones (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, Open-Qwen2VL 2B), showing simultaneous data/token efficiency (up to ~80% fewer active tokens) and performance improvements on both vision-understanding and hallucination benchmarks.

Thorough comparison with diverse existing debiasing baselines (training-free: VCD, PAI, VAR; training-based: LACING), demonstrating that VIG is competitive and largely orthogonal/complementary to these methods when combined.

Comprehensive ablations (selection ratio sweep, sample-only vs. sample+token selection, long-tail/task-distribution analysis, text-only benchmark preservation, attention-fraction and 'blind faith in text' robustness analysis) that collectively support the central claims and show limited unintended side effects.
Good reproducibility: detailed appendix with hyperparameters, thresholds, compute budgets, and qualitative examples, which should allow replication.
weaknesses: The core 'no-vision' condition is simulated via Gaussian-blurred images rather than true text-only input; the blurred image still passes through the vision encoder and adapter, so residual low-level visual cues (color histograms, brightness, rough layout) may leak into qQ(), potentially under/over-estimating VIG. No ablation of blur strength or comparison against alternative null-image baselines (e.g., black/noise image, fully masked visual tokens) is provided to validate this design choice.

VIG computation and the selective-training pipeline rely on a distinct 'post-pretraining, pre-instruction-tuning' checkpoint that cleanly separates alignment and instruction-tuning stages; this two-stage assumption does not directly apply to many modern LVLM training recipes (e.g., end-to-end or multi-stage interleaved training), limiting out-of-the-box applicability beyond the LLaVA-style pipeline, which the authors partially acknowledge as a limitation.

Reusing the same threshold τp for both sample- and token-level selection is a convenient but somewhat ad hoc design choice; while motivated by hyperparameter simplicity, no ablation decouples the two thresholds to show whether independent tuning would yield further gains or whether the coupling is actually near-optimal.

Experiments are restricted to moderate-scale, relatively dated backbones (LLaVA-1.5, ShareGPT4V, Open-Qwen2VL); no results on larger or more modern/stronger LVLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL-class models) are reported, so it is unclear whether the gains persist for already strongly-aligned, state-of-the-art models with less headroom for visual grounding improvement.

Results are reported as single-run numbers without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the (sometimes modest) gains, especially on benchmarks like DocVQA or CHAIR where improvements are small.

The token-level masking strategy (computing gradients only on high-VIG tokens within a sequence) could in principle affect fluency or coherence of function-word generation, but this potential side effect is not directly probed with fluency/perplexity-on-held-out-text metrics beyond the general text-only benchmarks used.
